analysis:
The UPA Common Minimum Programme (May 2004) committed the government to 'immediately enact a National Employment Guarantee Act' giving a legal guarantee of at least 100 days of employment to one able-bodied person in every rural, urban poor and lower middle class household. In the July 2004 budget speech the Finance Minister said the object was to guarantee 100 days of employment in a year to one able-bodied person in every poor household.

Parliament passed the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act in August 2005 and it came into force in February 2006; the law guarantees at least 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work. The core promise was therefore delivered.

The enacted law narrowed the scope to rural households, so the CMP's reference to urban poor and lower middle class households was not covered by the entitlement. Implementation data also show that the household-level guarantee of 100 days was not always met; the number of households that worked fell from 5.26 crore in 2009-10 to about 4.79 crore in 2013-14, and average days per household were below 100.
